title: WannaCry — the $10 off switch that saved the hospitals

scenes.label: The day the screens turned red
scenes.narration: [serious] Friday, May 12, 2017. In hospitals across England, computer screens suddenly go red. Patient files won't open. A message demands money. Soon, the same thing is happening all over the world. And the person who slows it down isn't a cop or a spy. [softly] He's a 22-year-old in a little beach town, with $10.69 and a lot of curiosity. But to see how this started, we have to go back two months.

visuals.at: isn't a cop or a spy

scenes.label: March: a fix nobody installed
scenes.narration: [calmly] It's March 2017. Microsoft fixes a weak spot in Windows, the software that runs most office computers. Tech people call a fix like this a patch. Think of it as a new lock for a broken door. In Britain, most hospitals are run by the NHS. That's the country's free, government-run health service. In March and April, it warns hospitals to install the fix. But plenty of computers never get it. Some still run Windows XP, a version so old that Microsoft had stopped fixing it.

visuals.at: a new lock for a broken door
plenty of computers never get it

scenes.label: April: a spy tool gets loose
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Then, in April, something strange happens online. A mystery group calling itself the Shadow Brokers dumps a pile of hacking tools on the internet. The tools are said to come from the NSA, America's biggest spy agency. One tool is called EternalBlue. It sneaks in through that same weak spot in Windows. Any computer without the March fix is at risk. Now anyone can grab it. A few weeks later, someone does.

visuals.at: dumps a pile of hacking tools

visuals.query: National Security Agency headquarters Fort Meade

scenes.label: Friday: WannaCry wakes up
scenes.narration: [serious] Now it's Friday, May 12. The attack begins. It's called WannaCry. It's ransomware, a program that locks up your files and holds them hostage. To get them back, you're told to pay $300 in bitcoin, a kind of digital money. But WannaCry has a nasty trick. It uses EternalBlue to jump from computer to computer by itself. Nobody has to click a bad link. [ominously] One sick machine can quietly infect the whole office.

scenes.label: Hospitals in trouble
scenes.narration: [worried] By that afternoon, England's hospitals are in real trouble. Staff are locked out of their computers. Appointments get canceled. At five emergency rooms, ambulances have to be sent somewhere else. In the end, at least 81 hospital groups are hit. So are nearly 600 family doctor offices. Picture walking into a hospital, and the computers just... don't work. And the attack is still spreading.

scenes.label: Then the whole world
scenes.narration: [urgently] And it's not just Britain. That same Friday, Spain's big phone company, Telefónica, tells workers to shut down their computers. FedEx gets hit too. Within a day, so do Renault car factories in France and Germany's national railway. Phones, packages, cars, trains. Everything runs on computers. And WannaCry keeps jumping from country to country. Who could possibly stop it?

scenes.label: Meet the guy on his week off
scenes.narration: [warmly] Now meet Marcus Hutchins. He's 22, and he lives with his family in Ilfracombe, a seaside town in England. He loves to surf. Online, people know him as MalwareTech. He hunts bad software for a security company in Los Angeles, working from his bedroom. This is supposed to be his week off. That Friday, he wakes up around 10 and goes to lunch with a friend. When he gets home at about 2:30, his computer is flooded with messages. The health service is under attack.

visuals.at: a security company in Los Angeles

scenes.label: A strange web address
scenes.narration: [curious] Marcus gets a copy of WannaCry and looks inside. He spots something odd. Before it does any damage, it tries to visit a web address. The name is a long string of random letters. And nobody owns it. So Marcus buys it, for $10.69. He does this a lot with addresses he finds in bad software. It shows him where an attack is spreading. [softly] As he said later, "The intent was to just monitor the spread."

scenes.label: The accidental off switch
scenes.narration: [surprised] The moment the address goes live, it lights up. Thousands of infected computers check in every second. Then Marcus and his team work out what it means. [pause] Every copy of WannaCry was asking one question. Is this address out there? If the answer was no, it attacked. If the answer was yes, it stopped. [dramatically] By buying it, Marcus had flipped an off switch. In his words, "we actually stopped the spread just by registering the domain."

scenes.label: Too late for some
scenes.narration: [sad] But the switch had a limit. It couldn't unlock computers that were already locked. It could only stop new ones. So timing decided who got hurt. The north of England, the Midlands and the East were hit early that Friday, before the switch. Of the 37 hospital groups that got fully locked out, 32 were there. On America's East Coast, it was still morning. Marcus's boss later told NBC News he had "saved the United States."

scenes.label: The weekend fight for the switch
scenes.narration: [serious] Then a new problem. The switch only works while the address stays online. If it goes down, sleeping copies of WannaCry could wake up. On Saturday morning, someone aims the Mirai botnet at it. That's a huge army of hacked gadgets, like home cameras and routers. They flood the address with junk traffic. [breathless] Marcus and his team fight to keep it up. It holds. In its first two days, the switch stops about a million infections. By then, Marcus has been awake for more than 30 hours.

visuals.at: a huge army of hacked gadgets

scenes.label: Microsoft breaks its own rule
scenes.narration: [curious] Microsoft is scrambling too. That Saturday, it does something unusual. It sends out a free fix for Windows XP, the old version it had stopped supporting. The next day, its president, Brad Smith, points a finger at governments. He says they hoard hacking tools instead of reporting the weak spots. He compares the leak to the military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen. Meanwhile, the attackers were waiting to get paid.

scenes.label: A ransom that flopped
scenes.narration: [calmly] By Sunday, Europol, Europe's police agency, counts about 200,000 victims in 150 countries. Its boss is worried about Monday, when millions of people go back to work. But the ransom turns into a flop. Most victims don't pay. By one early count, the attackers collected only about $55,000. Not a single hospital group in England paid. That same week, reporters find Marcus. He shrugs off the praise. "I'm definitely not a hero," he says.

scenes.label: From hero to handcuffs
scenes.narration: [serious] Three months later, in August 2017, Marcus flies to Las Vegas for a big hacker conference. As he heads home, the FBI arrests him at the airport. It's not about WannaCry. It's about different bad software, a bank-stealing program called Kronos. Prosecutors say he helped make it years earlier, as a teenager. [slowly] The young man who helped save the world is suddenly facing charges in America. And the big question is still open. Who built WannaCry?

scenes.label: The trail leads to North Korea
scenes.narration: [serious] In December 2017, the White House gives an answer. Tom Bossert, the president's homeland security adviser, says the US government believes North Korea did it. He calls the attack "cowardly, costly and careless." Britain agrees. Then, in September 2018, the Justice Department charges a North Korean programmer named Park Jin Hyok. Prosecutors say he worked for a fake company that served North Korea's military spies. He's still only accused. He has never faced trial.

visuals.at: the White House gives an answer

visuals.query: Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building
FBI wanted poster Park Jin Hyok

scenes.label: The bill, and the $10 hero
scenes.narration: [reflective] And Marcus? He pleads guilty. In July 2019, a judge gives him time served. No prison. Britain later added up the damage. WannaCry cost its health service about $120 million and some 19,000 canceled appointments. That's about one for every seat at Madison Square Garden. [long pause] [softly] The fix had been out for two months. In the end, what saved the day was a surfer, a weird web address and $10.69. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

visuals.at: had been out for two months

facts.claim: WannaCry was released worldwide on Friday, May 12, 2017.
At least 81 of 236 NHS trusts in England were affected, plus 603 other organizations including 595 GP practices.
Five A&E departments had to divert patients.
All infected NHS organizations ran unpatched or unsupported Windows; NHS Digital issued alerts in March and April 2017.
Trusts were told in 2014 to have robust plans to move off Windows XP by April 2015.
Amyas Morse: the attack 'could have been prevented by the NHS following basic IT security best practice.'
32 of the 37 trusts locked out were in the North and Midlands & East regions, hit before the kill switch.
No NHS organization paid the ransom.
Roughly 200,000 victims in at least 150 countries within 48 hours; ransom $300 in bitcoin; 192 victims had paid 31.7 BTC (about $55,490).
Telefónica, FedEx, Deutsche Bahn, Renault, China National Petroleum Corporation and Iranian universities were affected; Wainwright quote.
WannaCry used EternalBlue, a leaked NSA tool released by the Shadow Brokers in early 2017.
Microsoft patched supported systems in March (MS17-010) and released an emergency XP patch on May 13, 2017; Brad Smith compared the leak to stolen Tomahawk missiles.
Hutchins registered the domain for $10.69; it registered thousands of connections per second; quotes on monitoring the spread.
Hutchins worked from his bedroom for Kryptos Logic; CEO Salim Neino said he 'not only saved the United States'.
Mirai botnet attacked the sinkhole the next morning; Hutchins awake 30+ hours; kill switch prevented about a million infections from triggering in two days.
Hutchins arrested August 2017 in Las Vegas over Kronos; sentenced July 26, 2019 to time served and one year supervised release by Judge Stadtmueller.
Bossert attributed WannaCry to North Korea: 'cowardly, costly and careless'; 'These disruptions put lives at risk'; UK's Ben Wallace 'as sure as possible'.
Park Jin Hyok charged in 2018; Chosun Expo front; damage 'hundreds of millions, if not billions'.
February 2021 indictment adds Jon Chang Hyok and Kim Il; RGB units known as Lazarus Group; Demers quote.
DHSC estimated WannaCry cost the NHS £92 million and 19,000 appointments.
Hutchins, 22, lives with his family in Ilfracombe, a seaside town in England, is an avid surfer, works from his bedroom; 'I'm definitely not a hero.'

On May 12 (his week off) Hutchins woke around 10 AM, went to lunch with a friend, returned home about 2:30 to news of NHS systems being hit, then registered the unregistered domain the sample queried.

Brad Smith (May 14, 2017): 'An equivalent scenario with conventional weapons would be the U.S. military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen'; governments should report vulnerabilities rather than stockpile them.
Shadow Brokers leaked EternalBlue in April 2017.

seo.youtube_title: How WannaCry Was Stopped: The $10 Web Address That Saved Hospitals
seo.youtube_description:
How was WannaCry stopped? The true story of the 2017 ransomware attack that froze hospitals in England, and the $10.69 web address that shut it down.
A WannaCry documentary: a leaked NSA hacking tool, a surfer working from his bedroom, and North Korea.

On Friday, May 12, 2017, a program called WannaCry started locking up computers and asking for $300 in bitcoin. It spread by itself from computer to computer, using EternalBlue, a hacking tool said to come from the NSA that leaked online a month earlier. In England, at least 81 hospital groups and nearly 600 family doctor offices were hit. Five emergency rooms had to send ambulances elsewhere. Within two days, about 200,000 victims in 150 countries were counted. Microsoft had released the fix two months before.

That afternoon, Marcus Hutchins, a 22-year-old in a seaside town in England, found a strange web address inside the code and bought it for $10.69. By accident, he had flipped WannaCry's off switch. Three months later, the FBI arrested him over different malware. The US and UK governments say North Korea was behind WannaCry, and the Justice Department has charged a North Korean programmer, who is still only accused.
